div.p: AUTOSAR (AUTomotive Open System ARchitecture) provides an open and standardized E/E architecture for automobiles. AUTOSAR systems exhibit real-time requirements, i.e., an AUTOSAR application must always be schedulable. In this paper, we propose an overhead-aware method to find schedulable design configurations for an AUTOSAR application. We show how to construct a timing model for the application, discuss how to quantify the overheads of an AUTOSAR stack implementation, and assess their impact on timing and schedulability. We demonstrate the proposed method on an automotive case study and evaluate the effects of different types of overheads using synthetic applications.

div.head: CCS Concepts
div.p: •Computer systems organization → Real-time system architecture; Real-time operating systems; •Software and its engineering → Real-time systems software;

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Software applications in the automotive industry often exhibit real-time requirements. For example, if the ABS (Anti-lock Braking System) application fails to produce actuation commands within a specific time window (deadline), the breaks of the vehicle will not be applied on time. To guarantee such timing requirements, the application functionality is typically partitioned into a set of tasks, which are scheduled by an Operating System (OS) according to assigned priorities and activated either periodically, or based on external events with defined minimum inter-arrival time. Based on such information and bounds on the worst-case execution time of each task, a schedulability analysis [12] can then be applied to guarantee that the system is schedulable, i.e., every task finishes executing by its deadline.

DAC'17, June 18-22, 2017, Austin, TX, USA standardize an open software E/E architecture for automobile Electronic Control Units (ECU). Application functionality is implemented using software components. A software component comprises one or more runnables, which implement the application logic. The design must also specify a system configuration, which maps runnables to tasks, defines events (such as timers) used to activate tasks, and specifies the set of system services required by the application. Based on the configuration, vendor-provided tools are used to generate a customized AUTOSAR stack. The stack provides all functionalities required to access hardware devices, communicate between runnables, and schedule the application's tasks using a real-time OS. Runnables access system services through API functions in the automaticallygenerated Runtime Environment (RTE). All these facilities come with overhead cost added by the AUTOSAR stack. Unfortunately, this overhead is generally overlooked during the design process and performance testing in the early stages of the application development. In practice, we find that the overhead can be large enough to significantly affect the schedulability of AUTOSAR applications, especially for ECU employing small microcontrollers.

To address this problem, in this paper we propose a novel design method with the goal of finding schedulable design configurations for an AUTOSAR application in the early stages of its development (Section 3). In particular, in Sections 4, 5 we show how to model all sources of overhead for the application and check its schedulability. Our approach relies on MAST (Modeling and Analysis Suite for Real Time Applications) [5], an open source toolset for modeling and schedulability analysis. We then demonstrate our proposed method in Section 6 by measuring the overheads for an existing AUTOSAR stack, and we assess schedulability for both a small-scale case study and larger-scale synthetic applications. Finally, we conclude in Section 7.

div.head: RELATED WORK
div.p: To enrich an AUTOSAR configuration with timing information required for schedulability analysis, TADL2 (Timing Augmented Description Language) has been developed under the TIMMO-2-USE project [10]. TADL is capable of symbolic timing expression modeling, timing constraint specifications, and probabilistic timing information. Later versions of AUTOSAR have introduced timing extensions inspired by this project to specify the timing requirements of the application. Hladik, et al. [6] have analyzed a subset of AUTOSAR OS specifications from the schedulabil-Figure 1: Steps of the proposed method ity perspective. They concluded that the timing protection and scheduling tables in AUTOSAR OS extensions correspond to the pre-existing concepts of real-time scheduling theory. Also, existing methodologies of real-time scheduling theory can be used for analysis of AUTOSAR applications, mainly because these applications essentially use the scheduling services provided by the AUTOSAR OS, which is implemented by following the specification. Moghaddam [8] has performed a study of overheads for AUTOSAR systems, focusing mainly on comparison of inter-core and intra-core communication overheads. The work focuses on quantifying a specific source of overhead and does not provide support for design space exploration.

The closest related work is presented in [1], which discusses an approach for schedulability analysis of AUTOSAR applications. Similar to our approach, the authors rely on MAST for application modeling and analysis. They propose to include the RTE execution time and all other overheads in the application execution time. However, as we demonstrate in this paper, stack overheads are highly dependent on the application configuration. Hence, this approach requires regenerating the AUTOSAR stack and re-measuring tasks' execution times for each tested configuration.

div.head: PROPOSED METHOD
div.p: Figure 1 summarizes our proposed method. In contrast to [1], our goal is to support efficient design space exploration of schedulable configurations for a target AUTOSAR application. Therefore, we propose to separately estimate the execution time of application logic, and the overheads introduced by the AUTOSAR stack. For a chosen configuration, we then generate a MAST model which combines the timing of the application's runnables with the overheads specific to that configuration. This allows us to quickly yet precisely estimate the timing performance for a new configu-ration without the need to actually perform code generation and another set of (time consuming) measurements.

In the first step of the method, the chosen AUTOSAR stack implementation is analyzed to derive a table of worst case overhead values, similar to Table 2 in Section 6. We distinguish between two types of overheads: 1) the majority of considered overheads depend on both the stack implementation and ECU architecture, but are independent of the application. 2) Some overheads depend on the application implementation. For example, communication time depends on the size of exchanged messages. In this case, the overhead is expressed as a parametric function, in the example based on message size. The value of the parameter is then derived based on the configuration. In either case, overheads must be characterized once for each AUTOSAR stack and ECU that the designer wishes to explore, but can then be reused across applications. The second step involves measuring the running time of application logic on the selected ECU. In particular, the designer needs to determine the worst case execution time of each runnable, excluding the time required to execute RTE calls, since the latter varies based on the configuration. Finally, in the third step we use the previous information to perform schedulability analysis for a chosen configuration. We assume that the configuration is either selected manually or as a part of an automatic/semi-automatic design exploration process. The configuration is then translated to a MAST model including both runnable times and system overheads. Next, we run MAST on the model. If the performance is not satisfactory or the designer wants to explore more configurations, the MAST output can be used as input to decide on the next configuration. Otherwise, this configuration is selected as final and can be followed in the rest of the application development.

div.head: AUTOSAR STACK OVERHEADS
div.p: AUTOSAR stack overhead mainly comes from various services used by the application or the management done to run the application, e.g., process context switch, IO. It can be divided into following categories: OS Overheads: These involves operations required to manage the execution of tasks and device drivers; an example is shown in Figure 2(a). The system timer is used to generate periodic events; it interrupts the currently executing task every fixed period (timer tick). A higher-priority task can be allowed to preempt a lower-priority task; this generates context-switch overhead. Finally, for each Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) we account for interrupt entry and exit overheads, depending on the type of the ISR (AUTOSAR category 1 or 2). Communication Overheads: An AUTOSAR application uses API functions provided by the AUTOSAR RTE for communication; the considered overhead is the execution time of such functions, which depends on the communication type and the mapping of communicating runnables (i.e., same task/different tasks). AUTOSAR supports two main types of communication: 1) Implicit or Explicit Sender-Receiver: in implicit communication, all data read by a runnable is copied to its local environment before starting its execution and all the values written by it are written from its local environment after its execution is finished; in the case of explicit communication, all data is assumed to be written and read instantly upon performing the corresponding RTE call. Sender-receiver communication can further be queued

div.head: SCHEDULABILITY MODEL
div.p: The MAST model for an AUTOSAR system must capture: 1) ECU and hardware resources; 2) AUTOSAR stack; 3) AUTOSAR application. Table 1 details the mapping of all the major elements of the system to their corresponding MAST model elements. Due to space limitations, we We consider an AUTOSAR application composed of two tasks. The first task comprises runnables R1 and R2, and the second task runnable R3. R1 is activated periodically while R2 and R3 are activated by events, such as communication, generated by R1 and R2, respectively. The two events imply precedence constraints, meaning that R2 and R3 can only start executing after R1 and R2 complete, respectively. Additionally, R2 has a timing constraint that it should finish its execution in time TC1.

Under MAST, R1 is modeled as the Timed Activity of type Event Handler Timed_Activity_1, which is activated by External Event Ex_Event_1 of type Periodic. R2 and R3 are modeled by activities Activity_2 and Activity_3. The events generated by R1 and R2 that activate R2 and R3 are modeled as Internal Events In_Event_1 and In_Event_2. In_Event_3 represents the completion of R3. The timing requirement of R2 is modeled using a Timing Requirement element Timing_Req_1 associated with the generation of the event In_Event_2; its Deadline attribute is set to the value TC1. Runnable to task mapping is represented using the two Scheduling Server elements Sch_Server_1 (R1 and R2) and Sch_Server_2 (R3). Since the three runnables / two tasks are executed one after the other in sequence, they are mapped to the same Transaction, which represents an independent concurrent entity.

Each activity is further composed of multiple operations, each with a specified worst case duration. Different operations are used to represent the execution time of the corresponding runnable, and the associated overhead components (communication, service and runnable overheads), based on their relative execution order as shown in the examples of Figure 2. OS overheads are specified at the top level of the MAST model (Processing Resource and Scheduler), since they equally affect all tasks in the system. For checking the schedulability of the application, the MAST model is executed using offset-based response time analysis [11,12], which considers the effects of precedence constraints. The analysis returns the WCRT (Worst Case Response Time) for each activity or transaction, which is checked against any related deadline constraint, as well as the corresponding slack, which is the percentage by which we can increase the execution time while keeping the system schedulable.

div.head: EVALUATION
div.p: In this section, we first quantify the overheads for Arctic Core, an existing AUTOSAR stack implementation produced by ArcCore [2]. We then demonstrate the proposed method on the case study of a Front Light Management application. Finally, we study the effects of different types of overheads in more details based on synthetic applications.

div.head: Stack Overhead Results
div.p: We evaluated stack overheads based on the discussion in Section 4 on a STM32F 107VC ECU [9], which implements an ARM Cortex-M3 processor running at 72Mhz. To produce precise results, we analyzed the OS and RTE code generated based on varying configurations, and measured timing using a logic analyzer. However, other estimation methods could be used, including measurements using CPU performance counters or static timing analysis.

Table 2 summarizes results for a subset of non-parametric overheads, which are relevant for the rest of the evaluation. Parametric overheads include context switch, which depends on the number of tasks in the system, and communication. To improve the of the analysis, we split communication API functions in three parts, where the middle one is executed in mutual exclusion (critical section) and is the only part dependent on the message size. As an example, Figure 4 shows the worst case critical section length for explicit sender-receiver communication with message sizes between 1 Byte and 4 KB. Note that the measured overhead increases linearly with the message size, which is expected.

div.head: Case Study: Front Light Management
div.p: The considered application implements the functionality to manage head-light, daytime light, left and right indicator in the front part of the vehicle. Two buttons and two switches are connected to the ECU and used to control the four lights. Source code is available at [4]. This application has five main runnables in four software components:
1. otherSwitchStatusRunn and headLightSwitch-StatusRunn: These runnables are part of the same component and observe the status of the buttons.

div.head: lightRequestRunn:
div.p: This runnable manages the states of all the lights controlled through the buttons. Once the state is changed, lightRequestRunn sends the information of the mode and brightness of light to the frontLightManagerRunn runnable.

div.head: frontLightManagerRunn:
div.p: This runnable controls all lights except for the head-light, using the DIO service provided by the AUTOSAR stack. It forwards head-light control information to headLightRunn.

div.head: headLightRunn:
div.p: This runnable calculates the PWM (Pulse Width Modulation) duty cycle and controls the head-light by invoking the PWM service provided by the AUTOSAR stack.

Runnable lightRequestRunn invokes otherSwitchStatus-Runn and headLightSwitchStatusRunn using synchronized client-server communication; hence, all three runnables are mapped to the same task LightRequest. Runnables front-LightManagerRunn and headLightRunn are each mapped to tasks FrontLightManager and Headlight, respectively. Using the method described in Section 5, a MAST model for the Front Light Management application was created. The measured execution time for each runnable, including worst, average and best case, is presented in Table 3. Note that frontLightManagerRunn exhibits a significant difference between best and worst case timing, because its execution time is highly dependent on the state of the four lights. Since we are interested in guaranteeing that the application is schedulable under all conditions, for our results we used the worst case time for each runnable, but note that MAST can also produce results for average case timing. For each task, we set a deadline equal to its period, i.e., each activation of the task must finish before the next one. Finally, based on the number of tasks, we determined a worst case context switch overhead of 4559 CPU cycles.

To identify the effects of overheads, the model was executed twice -with and without all the overheads. Initially, we employed a button sampling period of 10 ms (72x10 4 cycles) to make system more responsive to driver commands. As shown in Tables 4 and5, the application is schedulable without overheads (all WCRTs are less than 10 ms). However, adding overheads increases the total CPU utilization by roughly 10%, resulting in an unschedulable system; no WCRT bound can be computed as the CPU utilization is over 100%. After analyzing the results, it was observed that the sampling period can be increased to 50 ms (36x10 5 cycles), which still provides sufficient responsiveness. The resulting configuration is schedulable as shown in the tables.

div.head: Synthetic Applications
div.p: We generated a large number of synthetic applications to evaluate the impact of configuration changes and various types of overheads on the schedulability of the system. Results are provided in Figure 5, where we vary the CPU utilization on the x-axis and plot the percentage of schedulable synthetic applications on the y-axis for the case where no overheads are consider, and the case where we include overheads based on the measured times in Section 6.1. For each point in the graph, we generated 2500 synthetic applications based on the parameter values shown in Table 6; in each figure, we then vary one parameter at a time. Where ranges are specified, we randomly assign the parameter value for each task according to a uniform distribution within the provided range. For each task, we set the deadline equal to its period and use rate-monotonic priority assignment [7], i.e., tasks with shorter period have higher priority. We further select random pairs of sender-receiver runnables in different tasks assuming non-queued explicit communication. We measured an average time of 432 ms to analyze one synthetic application for the default configuration, when executing MAST on a single core of an Intel i7-3740QM processor. Note that in Figures 5(b)-(f) we show a single graph for the no-overhead case, since changing the corresponding parameter has no impact on schedulability. However, varying the number of tasks in Figure 5(a) impacts both the nooverhead and the overhead case, since the schedulable utilization bound for rate-monotonic decreases with the number of tasks [7]. The drop in schedulability is much larger when overheads are considered: as the number of tasks increases, the total number of runnables, IO hardware operations and exchanged messages also becomes higher. Furthermore, the maximum number of context switches in a time window is also proportional to the number of tasks.

Of the remaining parameters, varying task periods has the largest impact on schedulability. For a constant utilization value, shorter periods correspond to shorter runnable execution times. Hence, the relative size of the overhead components becomes larger. The 1-10 ms case shows especially poor performance, which is expected as task periods approach the periodicity of the system timer, which is 1 ms in the tested system. On the other hand, varying the number of runnables per task in Figure 5(c) (while keeping the number of IO operations and messages per task constant) has little impact, since runnable overheads are small compared to the other overhead types. In conclusion, for the same design configuration and utilization factor, we observe that the number of schedulable applications is significantly lower when the system overhead is considered; this implies that ignoring the impact of overheads at the design stage can easily result in unsafe systems.

div.head: CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper, we presented an overhead-aware method to find schedulable design configurations for a given AU-TOSAR application. We quantified the overheads of an existing AUTOSAR stack and evaluated the proposed method using a sample AUTOSAR application. The presented case study, in addition to extensive experiments with synthetic applications, shows that overheads added by the AUTOSAR stack can have significant effects on the schedulability of the application. This suggests that considering added overheads in the early stages of the application development can save significant time and effort which could otherwise be wasted if the application is later found to be unschedulable.

Other Service Overheads: These include all other RTE provided services, such as I/O functionality. Similar to communication, the overhead is the execution time of the corresponding API function.Runnable Overheads: this is the overhead involved in executing a runnable as part of a task. It can be subdivided into four components: 1) Pre-Runnable-Event; 2) Post-Runnable-Event; 3) Pre-Runnable; 4) Post-Runnable. Pre-Runnable-Event overhead is the time consumed in executing the code from the event received by the task to the RTE function responsible for starting the runnable execution. Pre-Runnable overhead is the time taken by this RTE API function in starting the runnable. Similarly, Post-Runnable overhead is the time taken since runnable execution is finished and control reaches back to task through the RTE API functions, while Post-Runnable-Event overhead is the time taken to run the remaining task code till the execution enters a wait state for the next event.Figures2(b) and 2(c) depict overhead components for explicit and implicit sender-receiver communication, respectively, for the case of a task with two runnables activated by the same event. Note that the Pre-Runnable and Post-Runnable overheads for Runnable_2 are larger in Figure2(c) compared to 2(b), since they include the time required to receive/send data.
